title: Pinocchio sells his ABC book to go and see the puppet theatre.
paragraphs: Once the snow had stopped, Pinocchio set off along the road to school with his fine new ABC book under his arm: and as he went, his little head filled with a thousand plans and a thousand castles in the air, each more splendid than the last.
And talking to himself, he said:

“Today at school I’ll learn to read straight away: tomorrow I’ll learn to write, and the day after tomorrow I’ll learn to do sums. Then, with my skills, I’ll earn lots of money, and with the first money that comes into my pocket, I’ll get Dad a fine cloth coat at once. But why am I saying cloth? I’ll have it made entirely of silver and gold, with diamond buttons. And the poor man really deserves it; because, after all, to buy me books and let me learn, he was left in just his shirt… in this cold! Only dads can give up so much!…”
As he was saying this, full of feeling, he thought he heard music in the distance, pipes and the beats of a big drum: peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, boom, boom, boom, boom.
He stopped and listened. The sounds came from the far end of a very long side road leading to a little village built on the seashore.
“What can that music be? What a pity I have to go to school, otherwise…”
And he stood there, unable to decide. Still, he had to make a choice: either school or listening to the pipes.
“Today I’ll go and hear the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s always time for school,” the rascal said at last with a shrug.

No sooner said than done, he turned down the side road and began running as fast as he could. The farther he ran, the more clearly he heard the pipes and the thumps of the big drum: peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, boom, boom, boom, boom.
And there he was in the middle of a square full of people crowding around a large booth made of wood and canvas painted in a thousand colours.
“What’s that booth?” Pinocchio asked, turning to a boy from the village who was standing nearby.
“Read the sign, and you’ll know.”
“I’d gladly read it, but as it happens, today I can’t read.”
“You great ox! Then I’ll read it for you. You should know that the sign, in letters as red as fire, says: GRAND PUPPET THEATRE…”
“Has the play been going on long?”
“It’s starting now.”
“And how much does it cost to get in?”
“Four soldi.”
Pinocchio, burning with curiosity, forgot all self-control and said without shame to the boy he was talking to:
“Would you lend me four soldi until tomorrow?”
“I’d gladly lend them to you,” the other replied mockingly, “but as it happens, today I can’t.”
“I’ll sell you my jacket for four soldi,” the puppet said then.
“What would I do with a jacket made of flowery paper? If rain falls on it, you can’t get it off your back.”
“Do you want to buy my shoes?”
“They’re good for lighting a fire.”
“How much will you give me for my cap?”
“What a fine thing to buy! A cap made from the inside of a loaf! The mice might come and eat it right off my head!”
Pinocchio was on edge. He was about to make his last offer, but he could not find the courage: he hesitated, wavered, and suffered. At last he said:
“Will you give me four soldi for this new ABC book?”
“I’m a child, and I don’t buy things from children,” answered the little boy, who had more sense than he did.
“I’ll take the ABC book for four soldi,” called a second-hand clothes seller who had been there during the conversation.
And the book was sold on the spot. And to think that poor Geppetto had stayed at home, shivering in his shirtsleeves, to buy his son the ABC book!
